nameStory: Despite its name, Bermuda grass isn't actually from Bermuda! This world-traveling grass earned its common name because it became so abundant on the island of Bermuda after being introduced there. The scientific name Cynodon comes from Greek words meaning 'dog tooth,' referring to the sharp, pointed flower spikes that might remind you of a dog's canine teeth.
description: Bermuda grass is a low-growing, creeping grass that forms dense mats across the ground. It spreads by both underground stems (rhizomes) and above-ground runners (stolons) that root wherever they touch soil. The grass typically grows 4-6 inches tall in lawns but can reach up to a foot high when unmowed. Its distinctive flower heads look like tiny fingers radiating out from a central point, usually 3-6 spikes arranged like the spokes of a wheel.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive flower heads with 3-6 narrow, finger-like spikes radiating from a central point like tiny purple-tinged spokes of a wheel

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Short, narrow, blue-green to gray-green blades that feel somewhat rough and stiff to the touch, with a prominent white midrib running down the center

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, carpet-like mats that spread aggressively by underground stems and surface runners that root at joints

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Wiry, tough stems that are difficult to pull apart by hand, with visible nodes where leaves attach and roots may sprout

habitat: In New England, Bermuda grass is extremely rare and typically found only in the warmest, most protected locations like urban heat islands or near heated buildings. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, and cannot tolerate New England's harsh winters in most locations. You're most likely to spot it in disturbed areas, along roadsides, or in commercial landscapes in the region's warmest zones.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges late in spring when soil temperatures warm up, appearing as fresh green shoots from underground stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with active flowering from mid-summer through early fall, producing the characteristic finger-like seed heads.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until first frost, when the above-ground portions begin to turn brown and die back.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with all above-ground parts brown and dead, though underground stems may survive in protected locations.

funFact: Bermuda grass is so tough and persistent that NASA has studied it as a potential candidate for growing on Mars! Its ability to survive in harsh conditions and spread rapidly from tiny fragments makes it both a valuable turf grass in warm climates and a nightmare weed in gardens.
confusionNotes: The finger-like flower arrangement is quite distinctive and unlikely to be confused with other grasses. However, when not flowering, it might be mistaken for other creeping grasses, but Bermuda grass feels noticeably stiffer and more wiry than most lawn grasses.
contextualKnowledge: Bermuda grass goes by many names worldwide, including crabgrass in some regions (though this can be confusing since crabgrass usually refers to Digitaria species in North America). It's also called devil's grass, dog's tooth grass, and wiregrass, reflecting both its tenacious spreading habit and tough texture.
compareHints: Bermuda grass is the only Cynodon species commonly found in North America. Among other creeping grasses, it's distinguished by its unique wheel-spoke flower arrangement and exceptionally tough, wiry texture. Unlike softer lawn grasses like fescue or bluegrass, Bermuda grass stems resist tearing and have a distinctly rigid feel when handled.
